content: Many women prefer to have options for pain relief during labor and often wish to avoid invasive methods. Inhaled analgesia involves the self-administration of sub-anesthetic concentrations of agents, allowing the mother to remain awake with her protective laryngeal reflexes intact. These agents are generally easy to administer, can be initiated within a minute, and provide pain relief almost immediately. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of all forms of inhaled analgesia on both the mother and the newborn in cases where vaginal delivery was planned. The review included randomized controlled trials comparing inhaled analgesia with other inhaled agents, placebo, no treatment, or other non-pharmacological pain management methods. The review analyzed data from 26 studies involving 2,959 women. When comparing different types of inhaled analgesia, flurane derivatives were found to provide better pain relief than nitrous oxide during the first stage of labor. This was demonstrated by a lower pain intensity score (mean difference [MD] 14.39, 95% confidence interval [CI] 4.41 to 24.37, based on three studies with 70 women) and a higher pain relief score (MD -16.32, 95% CI -26.85 to -5.79, based on two studies with 70 women). However, there was significant variability in the results for both pain intensity (P = 0.003) and pain relief (P = 0.002), which raises concerns about the reliability of these findings due to the design of the included cross-over trials. Additionally, women in the nitrous oxide group experienced more nausea compared to those using flurane derivatives (risk ratio [RR] 6.60, 95% CI 1.85 to 23.52, based on two studies with 98 women). When comparing inhaled analgesia to placebo or no treatment, nitrous oxide provided greater pain relief (RR 0.06, 95% CI 0.01 to 0.34, based on two studies with 310 women; MD -3.50, 95% CI -3.75 to -3.25, based on one study with 509 women). However, nitrous oxide was associated with more side effects, including nausea (RR 43.10, 95% CI 2.63 to 706.74, based on one study with 509 women), vomiting (RR 9.05, 95% CI 1.18 to 69.32, based on two studies with 619 women), dizziness (RR 113.98, 95% CI 7.09 to 1833.69, based on one study with 509 women), and drowsiness (RR 77.59, 95% CI 4.80 to 1254.96, based on one study with 509 women). No significant differences were observed in outcomes when comparing different strengths of inhaled analgesia, different delivery systems, or inhaled analgesia with transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). Due to insufficient data, the review did not analyze outcomes such as the sense of control, satisfaction with the childbirth experience, mother-baby interaction, breastfeeding, admission to a special care baby unit, long-term infant outcomes, or costs. In conclusion, inhaled analgesia is effective in reducing pain intensity and providing pain relief during labor. However, significant variability was noted in the results for pain intensity. Nitrous oxide appears to cause more side effects, such as nausea, vomiting, dizziness, and drowsiness, compared to flurane derivatives or placebo. Flurane derivatives, on the other hand, are associated with more drowsiness than nitrous oxide. There is no evidence to suggest differences in outcomes when comparing different strengths of inhaled analgesia, delivery systems, or inhaled analgesia with TENS.
